description: Test data for a stability study (an invariance test) of the claim checker. Each row names one judged claim from one of the six gate texts and gives one piece of that claim's text exactly as it appears in the text's markdown file (md_original). That piece always sits on a single line of the file and never contains a citation marker. md_reworded says the same thing in different words: every fact, figure, name, quantity word, hedge and time frame is kept, so a correct checker should give the same verdict as before. md_negated exists only for claims the checker judged supported; it turns the cited fact into its opposite with the smallest edit that makes the cited source clearly fail to support it, so a correct checker should now say unsupported. To build a test text, replace md_original with md_reworded (or md_negated) in the markdown file and leave everything else unchanged. Known limit: paper1 is hard-wrapped, so its pieces cover only one line of a claim; when a claim cites two or more sources, another cited source may still back part of the changed sentence. Each negation_note says only which facts were turned round.

rows.md_original: after Rudolf died in 1291 the electors bypassed his son Albert for Adolf of Nassau, explicitly to forestall a hereditary Habsburg dynasty.
rows.md_reworded: after Rudolf's death in 1291 the electors passed over his son Albert in favour of Adolf of Nassau, explicitly to forestall a hereditary Habsburg dynasty.
rows.md_negated: after Rudolf died in 1291 the electors chose his son Albert over Adolf of Nassau, explicitly to secure a hereditary Habsburg dynasty.
rows.negation_note: The electors bypassing Albert to prevent a Habsburg dynasty was changed to choosing Albert to secure one; both halves were changed because changing one alone makes the sentence contradict itself.

rows.md_original: Bohemian kingship also legitimized itself through dynastic and sacral tradition centred on Saint Wenceslas's cult
rows.md_reworded: Bohemian kingship also drew its legitimacy from dynastic and sacral tradition centred on the cult of Saint Wenceslas

rows.md_original: decay fungi need moisture, oxygen, warmth, and a food source together, and the exposed end grain atop a post is where rainwater collects longest
rows.md_reworded: decay fungi require moisture, oxygen, warmth, and a food source at the same time, and rainwater collects longest on the exposed end grain at the top of a post

rows.md_original: a cross-culturally recurring practice of placing charged objects at a dwelling's vulnerable edges
rows.md_reworded: a practice, recurring across cultures, of placing charged objects at the vulnerable edges of a dwelling

rows.md_original: Early modern English witch bottles were stoneware or glass jugs filled with pins, nails, and bodily fluids, then heated and concealed near hearths and thresholds, attested from roughly the 1650s to at least 1705.
rows.md_reworded: Early modern English witch bottles were stoneware or glass jugs that were filled with pins, nails, and bodily fluids, then heated and hidden near hearths and thresholds; they are attested from roughly the 1650s to at least 1705.

rows.md_original: The popular claim that these bottles were preventive charms barring witches is not well supported by the surviving texts, which frame them chiefly as a cure applied once bewitchment was already suspected.
rows.md_reworded: The surviving texts give little support to the popular claim that these bottles were preventive charms barring witches, framing them chiefly as a cure applied once bewitchment was already suspected.
rows.md_negated: The popular claim that these bottles were preventive charms barring witches is well supported by the surviving texts, which frame them chiefly as a protection set up before any bewitchment was suspected.
rows.negation_note: The texts giving little support to the preventive-charm reading was changed to supporting it well, and the cure framing became a protection framing; both halves were changed because changing one alone makes the sentence contradict itself.

rows.md_original: A related Finnish tradition of hiding animal bones, coins, and tools in thresholds shows the same anxiety, with witchcraft fears more pronounced in densely built towns than in looser settlements.
rows.md_reworded: A related Finnish tradition of hiding animal bones, coins, and tools in thresholds reflects the same anxiety, with fears of witchcraft more pronounced in densely built towns than in looser settlements.
rows.md_negated: A related Finnish tradition of hiding animal bones, coins, and tools in thresholds shows the same anxiety, with witchcraft fears less pronounced in densely built towns than in looser settlements.
rows.negation_note: Witchcraft fears being more pronounced in dense towns was changed to less pronounced.

rows.md_original: English museum surveys report a comparable concealment pattern at hearths and doorways.
rows.md_reworded: English museum surveys report a comparable pattern of concealment at hearths and doorways.
